lead: No piston ring seals perfectly. On every compression and power stroke a little gas slips past the rings into the crankcase; this gas is called blow-by. Left there, it pressurises the crankcase, pushes oil out of the seals, and fills the oil with water, acid and fuel. Crankcase ventilation is the system that sweeps blow-by out of the crankcase. Old engines let it out to the air; every modern petrol car sends it back into the intake through a positive crankcase ventilation (PCV) valve so that it is burnt in the cylinders.
prereq: You need: rings and the sump from Lubrication systems and engine friction, and oil ageing (TAN, sludge) from Lubricants: properties and additives.

sections.h3: Blow-by: what gets into the crankcase

blocks.text: Blow-by leaks through the ring end gaps and past the ring faces when cylinder pressure is high. In a petrol engine it is partly unburnt mixture, pushed down during compression, and partly burnt gas, pushed down during combustion. It carries carbon dioxide, water vapour, carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, petrol vapour, soot and a fine oil mist. Worn rings or a scored liner make much more of it, so blow-by flow is a standard measure of engine wear.

An unventilated crankcase suffers four ways. Pressure builds and pushes oil out past the seals and gaskets. Water vapour condenses on cold walls and, with oil and soot, forms a creamy sludge that blocks the pick-up strainer. Nitrogen and sulphur oxides dissolve in that water as acids that corrode bearings, so the oil TAN climbs. Petrol vapour dissolves in the oil and thins it. A steady flow of air through the crankcase cures all four.

V̇<sub>bb</sub> is the blow-by flow measured at the breather, in L/min; V̇<sub>air</sub> is the air flow into the engine, in L/min. For a four-stroke, V̇<sub>air</sub> = V<sub>d</sub> × (N/2) × η<sub>v</sub>, with V<sub>d</sub> the swept volume in litres, N the speed in rev/min and η<sub>v</sub> the volumetric efficiency.

sections.h3: Open breathers and the closed PCV system

blocks.text: Early engines used an open breather: a road draft tube ran from the crankcase to just below the car, and air rushing past at road speed sucked the gas out, with fresh air entering through a breather cap. It worked only when the car moved, and it emptied fuel vapour and oil mist into the air. Emission rules ended it on petrol cars from the early 1960s, beginning in California.

Positive crankcase ventilation closes the loop. A hose brings filtered fresh air from the clean side of the air cleaner into the rocker cover. The air sweeps down through the crankcase, mixes with the blow-by, and the mixture is drawn by manifold vacuum through the PCV valve into the intake manifold, below the throttle. The cylinders then burn it. An oil separator, a baffle box or a small cyclone in the rocker cover, throws the oil droplets out of the gas and drains them back to the sump before the gas reaches the valve.

Some syllabi separate a semi-closed system, whose filler cap still breathes to the air, from a fully closed one. In the fully closed system, blow-by beyond what the valve can pass flows back up the fresh-air hose into the air cleaner and is still burnt.

sections.h3: The PCV valve: flow set by manifold vacuum

blocks.text: The PCV valve is a tapered plunger in a small housing, held by a light spring. Manifold vacuum pulls the plunger towards the manifold end; the spring pushes it back. The gap left around the taper sets the flow, so the valve meters blow-by to match the engine condition.

head: Engine condition
Manifold vacuum
Plunger
Flow
rows: none; a flame cannot reach the crankcase
small: little blow-by, and the idle mixture must not go lean
largest opening; surplus blow-by returns through the air cleaner

blocks.text: The engine management counts on a known PCV flow at idle. A valve stuck open, or a split hose, adds unmetered air and leans the mixture. A valve stuck shut or clogged with sludge stops the sweep, and the crankcase pressure symptoms return: oil leaks, oil in the air cleaner and sludge under the filler cap.

A turbocharged petrol engine has vacuum in the manifold only at part load; under boost the manifold is above atmospheric, and gas would be forced backwards into the crankcase. So it has two paths, each with a check valve. At part load blow-by goes through the PCV valve into the intake manifold. Under boost that path shuts and blow-by is drawn into the compressor inlet, where the pressure is a little below atmospheric. Oil carried over this way coats the compressor and intercooler, so separation matters more on turbo engines.

A diesel has no throttle, so there is little manifold vacuum to drive a PCV valve, and its blow-by carries much more soot. Diesels use closed crankcase ventilation (CCV): blow-by passes through a coalescing filter that catches oil and soot, and a pressure-regulating valve holds the crankcase slightly below atmospheric while the cleaned gas is drawn into the compressor inlet.

examples.question: A 1.5 litre four-stroke petrol engine runs at 3000 rev/min with a volumetric efficiency of 0.85. A blow-by meter on the breather reads 25 L/min. Taking the blow-by density as 1.1 kg/m³ and its unburnt fuel content as 3 percent by mass, find (a) the air flow into the engine in L/min, (b) the blow-by as a percentage of that air, (c) the blow-by mass per hour, and (d) the fuel vapour an open breather would release in a two-hour drive at this condition.
steps: Intake strokes per minute for a four-stroke: N/2 = 3000/2 = 1500.
(c) 25 L/min × 60 min/h = 1500 L/h = 1.5 m³/h. Mass = 1.5 m³/h × 1.1 kg/m³ = 1.65 kg/h.
(d) Gas in two hours = 1.65 × 2 = 3.3 kg. Fuel vapour = 0.03 × 3.3 kg = 0.099 kg, about 99 g, released to the air by an open breather and burnt in the cylinders by a PCV system.
examples.answer: (a) 1912.5 L/min; (b) 1.31 percent; (c) 1.65 kg/h; (d) about 99 g of fuel vapour in two hours.

examples.question: At idle a petrol engine draws 10.0 kg/h of air through its air-flow sensor, and the control unit injects fuel for an air-fuel ratio of 14.7. A split PCV hose lets in another 1.5 kg/h of air that the sensor never sees. Find the fuel flow, the true air-fuel ratio and the excess-air ratio λ (actual ratio ÷ 14.7).
steps: Fuel injected for the measured air: ṁ<sub>f</sub> = 10.0 ÷ 14.7 = 0.680 kg/h.
λ = 16.9 ÷ 14.7 = 1.15, so the mixture is 15 percent lean: the idle runs rough, and the oxygen sensor sees the lean mixture and adds fuel until λ returns to 1.
examples.answer: Fuel 0.680 kg/h, true air-fuel ratio 16.9, λ = 1.15: a 15 percent lean idle.

traps: Blow-by is gas leaking past the piston rings into the crankcase. It is not an exhaust leak and not a valve leak.
The PCV valve passes least at idle, when vacuum is highest, and opens most at full load. Writing it the other way round loses the marks.
A road draft tube is an open system that vents to the air. PCV is a closed system that burns the blow-by in the cylinders.
Do not swap the faults: a valve stuck open gives a lean, rough idle; a valve stuck shut gives crankcase pressure, oil leaks and sludge.
In a turbo engine under boost, blow-by goes to the compressor inlet, not to the pressurised intake manifold.

quiz.q: Define blow-by and name three gases it contains.
quiz.a: Blow-by is the gas that leaks past the piston rings into the crankcase on compression and power strokes. It contains unburnt mixture or fuel vapour, carbon dioxide, water vapour (and CO, NOx and soot).

quiz.q: Name the main parts of a PCV system.
quiz.a: Fresh-air hose from the clean side of the air cleaner, rocker cover with oil separator, PCV valve, and the hose to the intake manifold below the throttle.

quiz.q: Why does the PCV valve pass only a small flow at idle?
quiz.a: At idle manifold vacuum is high and pulls the plunger in, leaving a small gap. The engine makes little blow-by at idle, and a large flow of unmetered gas would lean the idle mixture and make it rough.

quiz.q: Explain how an unventilated crankcase forms sludge and acid.
quiz.a: Water vapour in the blow-by condenses on cold crankcase walls, mixes with oil and soot into sludge, and dissolves nitrogen and sulphur oxides to form acids that attack bearings. A steady flow of fresh air carries the vapour out before it condenses.

quiz.q: A 1.2 litre four-stroke engine runs at 4000 rev/min with volumetric efficiency 0.90, and the blow-by meter reads 30 L/min. Find the blow-by as a percentage of intake air.
A car shows oil in the air-cleaner box and oil weeping from the crankshaft seals. Which PCV fault fits, and why?
quiz.a: A blocked or stuck-shut PCV valve. Blow-by cannot leave through the valve, so crankcase pressure rises; it forces gas and oil mist backwards up the fresh-air hose into the air cleaner and pushes oil past the seals. Clean or replace the valve and hoses.

beyond: Engines now carry crankcase pressure sensors so that on-board diagnostics can detect a disconnected PCV hose, and separators have grown into cyclones and electrically driven centrifuges. Cold-climate engines heat the PCV valve so water in it cannot freeze. Search terms: crankcase ventilation oil separator, blow-by meter, closed crankcase ventilation filter.
